Let me analyze this pair.

Side A (PMID 29221659): Meta-analysis of GLP-1 RA CVOTs. Claim: fatal and non-fatal MI, GLP-1 RA vs placebo, assertion "explicit_no_difference" — "No significant effect of GLP-1 receptor agonists was identified on fatal and non-fatal myocardial infarction..." (sentence 9). This is verified against the abstract.

Side B (PMID 37024129): Network meta-analysis. Claim: GLP-1 RA reduce non-fatal MI vs standard treatments, assertion "directional", estimate_direction "-", based on sentence 10: "The study confirmed the benefits of SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists in reducing cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, admission to hospital for heart failure, and end stage kidney disease."

Verification: Side A claim matches source. Side B claim matches source — sentence 10 says GLP-1 RA reduce non-fatal MI. Extraction seems correct.

Comparability: Same exposure class (GLP-1 receptor agonists), similar outcome (fatal and non-fatal MI vs non-fatal MI — slightly different: A includes fatal and non-fatal MI, B says non-fatal MI). Comparable contrast: GLP-1 RA vs placebo (A) vs GLP-1 RA vs standard treatments (B). Both are between-group comparisons of GLP-1 RA against control. Reference differs somewhat (placebo vs standard treatments), but standard treatments in these trials typically include standard care; this is a contextual difference but comparability seems adequate — both assess GLP-1 RA effect on MI.

Findings: A explicitly reports no significant effect on MI (explicit no-effect conclusion). B reports a benefit (reduction in non-fatal MI). This is not_replicated: one reports an effect, the other explicitly reports no effect.

Wait — is A's "No significant effect" an explicit no-effect conclusion? The wording: "No significant effect of GLP-1 receptor agonists was identified on fatal and non-fatal myocardial infarction..." This is a substantive no-effect statement ("no significant effect... was identified"), which per instructions counts as explicit no-effect/no-difference conclusion. The instruction says "The words 'not statistically significant' alone describe statistical evidence; they do not by themselves assert no effect." But "No significant effect was identified" — this is the authors' conclusion of no effect on that outcome. I think this qualifies as explicit no-effect. The assertion field says "explicit_no_difference". Yes.

So: A = no effect on MI; B = reduction in non-fatal MI. → not_replicated, factor none.

Outcome nuance: A is "fatal and non-fatal MI", B is "non-fatal MI". Sufficiently similar MI outcome. Also A comparator placebo, B standard treatments — contextual difference but both are GLP-1 RA vs control. The not_replicated branch has priority. Factor none unless a pertinent textual difference is specifically supported. Could the difference in comparator (placebo add-on vs standard treatments) explain? The instruction: "Use factor none unless a pertinent textual difference is specifically supported." Both abstracts describe their comparators; A: GLP-1 RA vs placebo; B: vs standard treatments. That's a textual difference, but is it pertinent/explanatory? Hmm. The not_replicated branch says use factor none unless a pertinent textual difference is specifically supported. I'll use factor none — the comparator difference is present but not clearly explanatory of the discordance; both are meta-analyses of RCTs in type 2 diabetes. Actually one could argue B includes more recent trials (2022 search) including possibly more GLP-1 RA trials. But not specifically supported as explanatory. Factor none.

verdict.label: not_replicated
verdict.rationale: Both claims verify against their sources. Side A (meta-analysis of four GLP-1 RA cardiovascular outcome trials vs placebo) explicitly concludes no effect on myocardial infarction: 'No significant effect of GLP-1 receptor agonists was identified on fatal and non-fatal myocardial infarction'. Side B (network meta-analysis vs standard treatments) reports a directional benefit: GLP-1 receptor agonists 'confirmed the benefits... in reducing cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction...'. The exposure class (GLP-1 receptor agonists), population (adults with type 2 diabetes), outcome domain (myocardial infarction), and between-group versus-control contrast are sufficiently similar to compare. One source explicitly reports no effect on MI while the other reports a reduction, so the finding is not replicated; this branch takes priority over any apparent contradiction. The comparator wording differs (placebo vs standard treatments) but neither abstract supports this as an explanation for the discordance, so no contextual factor is applied.

The study confirmed the benefits of SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists in reducing cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, admission to hospital for heart failure, and end stage kidney disease.
